title: Meeting the Family
description: Being a guest with a partner's family: greeting the parents, food offered again and again, the questions families ask, and taking leave properly.

phrases.registerNotes: Many city families have their children's friends and partners call the parents Om and Tante (from Dutch); others prefer Bapak and Ibu. Ask your partner which this family uses.
phrases.cultureNote: Greet the oldest first. Many families expect salim: take the elder's right hand and touch it lightly to your forehead or nose, as your partner does.

phrases.registerNotes: Pacar is a boyfriend or girlfriend; the -nya ties you to Dewi, as in temannya Dewi (Dewi's friend).
phrases.cultureNote: Some families are conservative about dating, and your partner may introduce you as a friend (teman) at first. Agree beforehand how you'll be introduced.

phrases.registerNotes: Say it after the greetings, and again as you leave. Terima kasih atas undangannya is a little more formal.

phrases.indonesian: Ini ada sedikit oleh-oleh dari Selandia Baru.
phrases.english: I've brought a little something from New Zealand.
phrases.registerNotes: Say it as you hand the gift over. Sedikit (a little) keeps it modest, which is the polite way to give.
phrases.cultureNote: Arriving with something is expected: oleh-oleh from home is ideal, or a box of cakes or fruit. Hand it over with your right hand, or both hands.

phrases.english: Oh, please don't go to any trouble.
phrases.registerNotes: Said when tea, snacks or a meal appear. It's politeness, not a refusal: the host carries on anyway, and you then accept with thanks.

phrases.english: Come on, eat up. Don't be shy.
phrases.registerNotes: What hosts say, often more than once; reply Iya, Tante, terima kasih and take some. Offering with di- is the usual pattern: Silakan diminum (please, have your drink).
phrases.cultureNote: Guests usually wait to be invited before eating or drinking what's put out. Once the host says silakan or ayo, go ahead.

phrases.registerNotes: Masakan is cooking, what has been cooked. Asking Ini masakan Tante sendiri? (Did you make this yourself?) is a compliment too.
Offer after the meal, especially to clear plates. The answer is usually Tidak usah, duduk saja (No need, just sit), but the offer is appreciated.

phrases.indonesian: Sudah, Tante, terima kasih. Saya sudah kenyang.
phrases.english: I'm fine, thank you. I'm full.
phrases.registerNotes: Sudah here is 'that's enough'. Expect to be urged more than once (Tambah lagi, have some more), and repeat it warmly each time.
phrases.pitfallNote: A plain Tidak, terima kasih sounds cold to a host; sudah kenyang gives a reason nobody can argue with.

phrases.registerNotes: When the host keeps insisting, accepting a small extra spoonful is often kinder than refusing a third time.

phrases.english: So when are you getting married?
phrases.registerNotes: You'll hear it, along with Kapan punya anak? (When are you having children?), as friendly interest rather than prying.
phrases.cultureNote: It's the stock question at family gatherings, Lebaran especially, and a smile and a light answer are all it needs.

phrases.english: Just keep us in your prayers.
phrases.registerNotes: The classic answer to Kapan nikah? and other questions about the future: warm, and it commits to nothing. Mohon doanya, Tante is a slightly more formal version.
You may hear it in the first conversations with a partner’s family, or from a neighbour. A simple factual answer is enough.
phrases.cultureNote: A normal question in Indonesia, where religion is on the ID card, not a rude one. From a partner's family it often has marriage in mind, since marrying across religions is difficult there, so agree with your partner how to answer.

phrases.english: I'll be off now, Uncle, Auntie.
phrases.registerNotes: Pamit is taking your leave properly; dulu ('first') softens it, as if you'll be back. Say it to each of the elders, not just to your partner.
phrases.cultureNote: Slipping away without pamit is rude. Hosts often protest (Kok buru-buru? Why the hurry?), so start saying goodbye a little before you mean to leave.
